legacy: Lewis Terman played a major role in the development of modern psychological assessment and intelligence research. His efforts to standardize cognitive testing helped establish measurement practices that influenced education, psychology, and talent identification programs for decades. His large-scale studies of gifted individuals also contributed valuable long-term data about human development, achievement, and educational outcomes.
earlyLife: Terman grew up in rural America and developed a strong interest in learning and education. His academic success encouraged him to pursue advanced studies in psychology at a time when the field was becoming increasingly scientific and data-driven. He became fascinated by individual differences in learning and intellectual performance, interests that would define much of his career.
majorContributions: Terman is best known for revising and expanding intelligence testing through the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale. His work helped establish systematic methods for measuring cognitive abilities and comparing performance across age groups. He also conducted one of the most influential longitudinal studies of gifted individuals, examining how cognitive ability relates to education, health, career success, and personal development across the lifespan.
laterLife: Throughout the later years of his career, Terman continued researching intelligence, education, and human achievement. He refined assessment methods, analyzed long-term developmental outcomes, and encouraged greater use of psychological measurement in education. His research generated extensive data that influenced psychologists, educators, and policymakers for many years.
whyImportant: Terman helped transform the measurement of cognitive abilities into a structured scientific enterprise. His work influenced educational assessment, talent identification, and psychological research worldwide. While some aspects of intelligence testing remain debated, many principles of standardized assessment and longitudinal research trace part of their development to contributions associated with his work.
